questions.why: Data being processed sits decrypted in memory, so enclaves and access controls protect it.

questions.q: Which data classification is usually the most restricted in a business?
questions.why: The most sensitive data, such as trade secrets or personal data, gets the strictest handling.

questions.q: What is the difference between a data owner and a data custodian?
options: The custodian sets policy; the owner backs it up
The owner is accountable for the data; the custodian handles day-to-day protection
questions.why: Owners, usually business leaders, decide classification and access; custodians implement it.

questions.q: What does a data processor do under privacy laws like GDPR?
options: Handles personal data on behalf of a controller
questions.why: The controller decides purposes; processors such as cloud providers act on its instructions.

questions.q: What is the right to be forgotten?
options: An individual's right to have their personal data erased
questions.why: Under GDPR, people can ask for their data to be deleted when there's no reason to keep it.

questions.q: What is wireless site surveying used for?
options: Mapping signal coverage and interference before or after deploying access points
questions.why: Surveys and heat maps show where coverage is weak, overlapping or leaking outside.

questions.q: Which Wi-Fi security mode uses 802.1X and a RADIUS server for individual logins?
questions.why: Enterprise mode authenticates each user, so one person leaving doesn't require changing a shared key.

questions.q: What is EAP-TLS?
options: An 802.1X method using certificates on both client and server
questions.why: Mutual certificates make EAP-TLS one of the strongest wireless authentication methods.

questions.q: What does MDM let a company do with a lost phone?
options: Locate, lock or remotely wipe it
questions.why: Remote wipe removes corporate data so it isn't exposed.

questions.q: Which mobile deployment model lets employees use personal phones for work?
questions.why: Bring your own device saves cost but makes control and privacy harder to balance.

questions.q: What is COPE?
questions.why: The company owns and manages the device but allows some personal use.

questions.q: What is containerisation on a mobile device?
options: Separating work apps and data from personal ones
questions.why: A work container can be wiped without touching personal photos and apps.

questions.q: What is input validation?
options: Checking that user input matches what is expected before using it
questions.why: Validating type, length and format blocks many injection attacks.

questions.q: What is code signing used for?
options: Proving software comes from a known publisher and hasn't been altered
questions.why: The publisher signs with a private key, and the OS checks the signature before running it.

questions.q: What is sandboxing for applications?
options: Running an app in a restricted environment that limits what it can access
questions.why: If a sandboxed app is compromised, the damage stays contained.

questions.q: What does static application security testing (SAST) analyse?
questions.why: SAST finds flaws early in development; DAST tests the running app.

questions.q: Why keep an asset inventory?
options: You can't protect or patch systems you don't know about
It is required for backups only
questions.why: An accurate inventory is the foundation for vulnerability management and incident response.

questions.q: What should happen to a hard drive at the end of its life if it held sensitive data?
options: Sanitise or destroy it and keep a certificate of destruction
questions.why: Documented sanitisation or destruction proves the data can't be recovered.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a vulnerability scan's CVSS score?
options: Rating how severe a vulnerability is
questions.why: CVSS scores from 0 to 10 help prioritise; context such as exposure also matters.

questions.q: What is a bug bounty programme?
options: Rewarding outside researchers who responsibly report vulnerabilities
questions.why: Bounties bring many testers to find flaws before criminals do.

questions.q: After a patch is applied, what confirms the vulnerability is fixed?
questions.why: Validation by rescan shows the fix took effect.

questions.q: What is an exception in vulnerability management?
options: A documented decision not to fix a vulnerability, often with compensating controls
questions.why: Exceptions record accepted risk with reasons and a review date.

questions.q: What does file integrity monitoring (FIM) detect?
questions.why: FIM compares files to known-good hashes and alerts when system files change.

questions.q: What does DNS filtering do?
options: Blocks access to known malicious or unwanted domains
questions.why: Requests for blocked domains fail or go to a warning page, stopping many threats early.

questions.q: What does a secure email gateway do?
options: Filters incoming and outgoing email for spam, phishing and malware
questions.why: Gateways scan attachments and links before mail reaches users.

questions.q: What does DKIM add to an email?
options: A digital signature proving the message came from the domain and wasn't altered
questions.why: Receivers check the signature against the public key published in the domain's DNS.

questions.q: What does XDR add beyond EDR?
options: Correlation of data from endpoints, network, email and cloud together
questions.why: Extended detection and response joins signals across many sources for better detection.

questions.q: What does user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) look for?
options: Unusual behaviour compared with each user's or device's normal pattern
questions.why: Deviations such as odd hours or unusual data volumes can reveal compromised accounts.

questions.q: What is a jump box (jump server) used for?
options: A hardened host admins connect through to reach sensitive systems
questions.why: Funnelling admin access through one monitored point reduces exposure.

questions.q: What does a privileged access management (PAM) tool do?
options: Controls, monitors and often provides temporary admin credentials
questions.why: PAM vaults admin passwords, grants just-in-time access and records sessions.

questions.q: What is just-in-time permissions?
options: Elevated access granted only when needed and removed afterwards
questions.why: Standing admin rights are a big risk; temporary elevation shrinks that window.

questions.q: What is federation in identity management?
options: Trusting identities from another organisation's identity provider
questions.why: Federation lets users log in to partner services with their home credentials.

questions.q: What does OAuth provide?
options: Delegated authorisation so an app can access resources without your password
questions.why: OAuth issues tokens with limited scope, such as letting an app read your calendar.

questions.q: What does OpenID Connect add on top of OAuth?
options: An authentication layer that confirms who the user is
questions.why: OIDC adds an ID token so apps can log users in, not just access their data.

questions.q: Which MFA method is most resistant to phishing?
questions.why: FIDO2 keys check the website's origin, so a fake site can't use them.

questions.q: Why is SMS considered a weak second factor?
options: Codes can be intercepted or redirected by SIM swapping
questions.why: Attackers who take over a phone number receive the codes.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a password manager?
options: Generating and storing unique strong passwords for every account
questions.why: Unique passwords stop one breach from exposing every account.

questions.q: What is passwordless authentication?
options: Logging in with something like a passkey or biometric instead of a password
questions.why: Passkeys use public-key cryptography, removing passwords that can be phished or reused.

questions.q: What is account provisioning?
options: Creating accounts and granting the right access when someone joins
questions.why: Good provisioning gives new staff the access their role needs from day one.

questions.q: Why must deprovisioning happen promptly when someone leaves?
options: So their access can't be misused after they've gone
questions.why: Former employees' active accounts are a common route for insider attacks and breaches.

questions.q: What does scripting and automation help security teams do?
options: Respond consistently and quickly to routine tasks
questions.why: Automation handles repetitive work such as account provisioning and ticket creation with fewer errors.

questions.q: What is a risk of too much automation?
options: A single faulty script can make widespread mistakes quickly
questions.why: Automated actions need testing and oversight because errors spread at machine speed.

questions.q: In incident response, what does eradication involve?
options: Removing the cause, such as malware and attacker access
questions.why: Eradication follows containment and must finish before recovery.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a tabletop exercise?
options: Walking through an incident scenario in discussion to test the plan
questions.why: Tabletops reveal gaps in roles and procedures without risk to systems.

questions.q: What is a legal hold?
options: An order to preserve data relevant to a legal matter
questions.why: Normal deletion stops for the covered data until the hold is lifted.

questions.q: What is e-discovery?
options: Finding and producing electronic information for legal proceedings
questions.why: Organisations must be able to search and hand over relevant emails and files.

questions.q: Which log source shows which websites users visited through the corporate proxy?
questions.why: Proxy logs record URLs, users and times for web traffic.

questions.q: Which log would show which IP address a laptop was given at a certain time?
questions.why: DHCP logs map MAC addresses to leased IPs and times, linking traffic to devices.

questions.q: What is a security policy?
options: A high-level statement of management's intent and requirements
questions.why: Policies say what must be done; standards and procedures say how.

questions.q: What is a standard in governance documents?
options: A mandatory requirement, such as a minimum password length
questions.why: Standards make policies measurable and enforceable.

questions.q: What is a procedure?
options: Detailed step-by-step instructions for doing a task
questions.why: Procedures such as onboarding steps make tasks consistent.

questions.q: What is a risk register?
options: A document listing identified risks, their ratings, owners and responses
questions.why: It tracks risks over time so they're managed, not forgotten.

questions.q: What is risk appetite?
options: How much risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its goals
questions.why: Appetite guides whether risks are accepted or must be reduced.

questions.q: What is a key risk indicator (KRI)?
options: A metric that warns when risk is increasing
questions.why: KRIs, such as a rising count of unpatched systems, give early warning.

questions.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative risk analysis?
options: Qualitative uses ratings like high or low; quantitative uses numbers such as money
questions.why: Quantitative uses values such as SLE and ALE; qualitative uses scales and judgement.

questions.q: What does a vendor risk assessment check?
options: Whether a supplier's security is adequate for the data or access they'll have
questions.why: Third parties with access to your systems or data extend your risk.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a right-to-audit clause in a contract?
options: It lets the customer inspect the vendor's security controls
It lets the vendor audit the customer
questions.why: Without it, customers may have no way to verify a supplier's claims.

questions.q: What is an SLA?
options: An agreement defining expected service levels such as uptime
questions.why: Service-level agreements set measurable targets and remedies if they're missed.

questions.q: What is an MOU?
options: A memorandum of understanding that states shared intent, usually not legally binding
questions.why: MOUs document cooperation without the detail or force of a contract.

questions.q: What is an attestation in compliance?
options: A formal statement, often by an auditor, that controls meet requirements
questions.why: Attestations such as SOC 2 reports give customers assurance.

questions.q: What is the difference between an internal and external audit?
options: Internal audits are done by the organisation's own staff; external by independent parties
questions.why: External audits carry independent credibility for regulators and customers.

questions.q: What is the consequence of non-compliance with regulations like GDPR?
options: Fines, legal action and reputational damage
questions.why: Regulators can impose large fines, and customers lose trust.

questions.q: Which penetration test type is done with full knowledge of the environment?
questions.why: Testers get diagrams, code and credentials to examine everything thoroughly.

questions.q: What is the main goal of security awareness training on phishing?
options: Teaching users to recognise and report suspicious messages
questions.why: Trained users report phishing quickly, giving the security team early warning.

questions.q: Why run phishing simulations?
options: To measure and improve how users respond to realistic phishing
questions.why: Simulations show who needs more training and track improvement over time.

questions.q: What should employees do when they spot a likely phishing email?
options: Report it using the approved method and not click anything
Reply to ask if it's real
Forward it to colleagues as a warning
questions.why: Reporting lets the security team block the sender and warn others.

questions.q: Which malware disguises itself as useful software to trick users into installing it?
questions.why: A Trojan relies on the user running it; it doesn't spread on its own like a worm.

questions.q: Which malware records every key a user presses?
questions.why: Keyloggers capture passwords and messages as they're typed, often sending them to the attacker.

questions.q: What is a remote access Trojan (RAT)?
options: Malware that gives an attacker hidden remote control of a system
questions.why: RATs let attackers browse files, run commands and watch the user without permission.

questions.q: What makes fileless malware hard to detect?
options: It runs in memory using legitimate tools like PowerShell and leaves few files on disk
questions.why: Scanners that look for malicious files on disk find little to catch.

questions.q: Which malware hides deep in the operating system to conceal itself and other malware?
questions.why: Rootkits alter the OS or firmware so normal tools can't see them.

questions.q: What is bloatware?
options: Unwanted pre-installed software that wastes resources and may add risk
questions.why: Vendor-installed extras increase the attack surface and should be removed.

questions.q: What triggers a logic bomb?
options: A specific condition, such as a date or an employee being removed from payroll
questions.why: Logic bombs lie dormant until their condition is met, often planted by insiders.

questions.q: Which malware spreads across networks by itself without user action?
questions.why: Worms exploit vulnerabilities to copy themselves from host to host.

questions.q: What is spyware?
options: Software that secretly collects information about a user's activity
questions.why: Spyware monitors browsing, keystrokes or location and sends data to a third party.

questions.q: What does ransomware typically demand payment in?
questions.why: Cryptocurrency is harder to trace, which suits criminals.

questions.q: What is RFID cloning?
options: Copying the data from an access badge to make a working duplicate
questions.why: Many proximity cards can be read from a short distance and copied to a blank card.

questions.q: What is an environmental attack on a data centre?
options: Targeting power, cooling or fire systems to disrupt operations
questions.why: Disabling HVAC or power can take systems offline without touching the network.

questions.q: What is a brute-force attack on a password?
options: Using a list of common words
Reading it from a sticky note
Tricking the user into revealing it
Trying every possible combination until one works
questions.why: Brute force is guaranteed eventually but slow against long passwords; lockouts slow it further.

questions.q: What is a dictionary attack?
options: Phishing with a fake dictionary site
Trying words and common passwords from a list
questions.why: Dictionary attacks are fast against weak, common passwords.

questions.q: Which practice best defends against password spraying?
options: MFA plus blocking commonly used passwords
questions.why: Spraying uses common passwords; MFA stops a correct guess from being enough.

questions.q: What is a cryptographic collision?
options: Two different inputs producing the same hash
questions.why: Collisions let attackers substitute content while the hash still matches, which breaks integrity checks.

questions.q: Which protocol securely replaces FTP for file transfers?
questions.why: SFTP runs over SSH and encrypts both credentials and data.

questions.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.why: HTTP uses port 80 in clear text; HTTPS wraps it in TLS on port 443.

questions.q: Which secure protocol is used to send email between servers with encryption?
questions.why: STARTTLS upgrades an SMTP connection to an encrypted one.

questions.q: Which port does LDAPS use?
questions.why: LDAP uses 389 in clear text; LDAPS wraps it in TLS on port 636.

questions.q: Which protocol provides secure time synchronisation features such as authentication?
questions.why: Accurate, trusted time matters for logs, certificates and Kerberos.

questions.q: What is DNSSEC?
options: Digital signatures on DNS records so responses can be verified
questions.why: DNSSEC protects integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality.

questions.q: What does DNS over HTTPS (DoH) protect?
options: The privacy of DNS queries from eavesdroppers
The integrity of DNS records on the server
questions.why: DoH encrypts the query, but it can also bypass corporate DNS filtering.

questions.q: Which VPN protocol suite works at the network layer and can protect all IP traffic between sites?
questions.why: IPsec is the standard for site-to-site VPNs.

questions.q: What is a clientless (SSL/TLS) VPN?
options: A VPN accessed through a web browser without installing client software
questions.why: Users reach web-based internal apps through a portal in their browser.

questions.q: What does SASE combine?
options: Network and security services delivered from the cloud
questions.why: Secure access service edge merges SD-WAN with cloud security such as SWG, CASB and ZTNA.

questions.q: What does SD-WAN do?
options: Intelligently routes traffic across multiple WAN links, such as broadband and MPLS
questions.why: Software-defined WAN picks the best path per application and reduces reliance on expensive circuits.

questions.q: What does a next-generation firewall add beyond port filtering?
options: Application awareness, user identity and intrusion prevention
questions.why: NGFWs can allow or block by application, such as permitting web browsing but not file sharing.

questions.q: What is a layer 7 firewall able to inspect?
options: Application data, such as HTTP requests
questions.why: Application-layer inspection catches attacks hidden inside allowed ports.

questions.q: What does a forward proxy do?
options: Makes requests to the internet on behalf of internal clients
Accepts requests from the internet for internal servers
questions.why: Forward proxies filter and log user web traffic. Reverse proxies sit in front of servers.

questions.q: What does a reverse proxy do?
options: Receives client requests and forwards them to internal servers
questions.why: It hides server details and can add TLS termination, caching and WAF protection.

questions.q: What is a security benefit of a load balancer?
options: It spreads traffic so no single server is overwhelmed and can absorb some attacks
questions.why: Load balancers improve availability and can hide backend servers.

questions.q: What does 802.1X provide on a wired network?
options: Port-based authentication before a device gets network access
questions.why: A device must authenticate, usually via RADIUS, before the switch port passes normal traffic.

questions.q: What is the role of a RADIUS server in 802.1X?
options: The authentication server that checks credentials
questions.why: The supplicant is the client, the authenticator is the switch or AP, and RADIUS is the authentication server.

questions.q: What does a NAC posture check verify?
options: A device's health, such as patches and antivirus, before granting access
questions.why: Non-compliant devices can be quarantined until they're fixed.

questions.q: What is the difference between agent and agentless NAC?
options: Agent NAC works only on phones
Agent NAC installs software on devices; agentless checks them without it
questions.why: Agents give deeper checks; agentless suits devices where software can't be installed.

questions.q: What does a TPM chip support?
options: Secure key storage and measured boot
questions.why: The TPM stores keys, such as BitLocker's, and records boot measurements.

questions.q: What does Secure Boot do?
options: Only allows boot software signed by trusted keys to run
questions.why: It stops bootkits that replace the boot loader with malicious code.

questions.q: What is measured boot?
options: Timing how long the boot takes
Recording hashes of each boot component so they can be checked later
questions.why: The TPM stores the measurements, which can be reported to a server for attestation.

questions.q: What is remote attestation?
options: A device proving its boot state and configuration to a remote server
questions.why: Using TPM measurements, the server can refuse access to devices that booted tampered software.

questions.q: What is a self-encrypting drive (SED)?
options: A drive that encrypts data in its own hardware
questions.why: SEDs encrypt everything automatically with little performance cost.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a firmware update for network devices?
options: Fixing vulnerabilities and bugs in the device's built-in software
questions.why: Routers and switches have firmware flaws too, so updates are part of patching.

questions.q: Why disable unused switch ports?
options: So no one can plug in an unauthorised device
questions.why: Unused live ports are an easy way into the network.

questions.q: What is port security on a switch?
options: Limiting which MAC addresses can use a port
questions.why: If an unknown MAC appears, the port can be shut down or the traffic dropped.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a VLAN?
options: Logically separating devices into different broadcast domains
questions.why: VLANs keep groups such as guests, voice and servers apart even on the same switch.

questions.q: What is a screened subnet?
options: The modern term for a DMZ between the internet and the internal network
questions.why: Public-facing servers sit there, separated from internal systems by firewalls.

questions.q: What is an air gap?
options: A system or network with no connection to other networks
A gap in a firewall rule
questions.why: Air-gapped systems can only be reached physically, though removable media is still a risk.

questions.q: Which cloud security control discovers which cloud apps employees are using?
questions.why: A cloud access security broker gives visibility into shadow IT and enforces policy on cloud services.

questions.q: What is a security group in a cloud environment?
options: A virtual firewall controlling traffic to cloud resources
A user group in Active Directory
questions.why: Security groups set allowed ports and sources for instances.

questions.q: What is a common cause of cloud data breaches?
options: Misconfigured storage, such as public buckets
questions.why: Storage left publicly readable exposes data without any hacking needed.

questions.q: What is responsibility under IaaS for patching the guest operating system?
questions.why: In IaaS the provider secures the hardware and hypervisor; the customer manages the OS and above.

questions.q: What is a hybrid cloud's main security challenge?
options: Keeping consistent security policies across on-premises and cloud environments
questions.why: Different tools and responsibilities in each environment can leave gaps.

questions.q: What is a container's main security consideration compared with a VM?
options: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel flaw affects all of them
questions.why: VMs isolate with separate kernels; containers rely on the shared host kernel.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an API gateway?
options: A central point that authenticates, rate-limits and routes API requests
questions.why: Gateways protect microservices from abuse and enforce consistent controls.

questions.q: What is rate limiting?
options: Limiting bandwidth for all users equally
Restricting how many requests a client can make in a period
questions.why: It slows brute-force, scraping and some DoS attacks.

questions.q: What does the principle of least functionality mean?
options: Systems run only the services and features they need
questions.why: Each unneeded feature is extra attack surface.

questions.q: What is configuration drift?
options: Systems gradually moving away from their approved baseline
questions.why: Untracked manual changes cause drift; automated configuration management detects and fixes it.

questions.q: What is a golden image?
options: A pre-hardened standard system image used to build new machines
A backup of a failed server
questions.why: Building from a golden image gives every system the same secure starting point.

questions.q: What does a host-based firewall protect?
options: The individual system it runs on
questions.why: It filters traffic to and from that host, even from other machines on the same network.

questions.q: What is the purpose of disabling autorun for removable media?
options: Stopping malware on USB drives from running automatically
questions.why: Autorun was a classic way for USB malware to spread.

questions.q: What does a data loss prevention (DLP) system do when an employee emails a file containing card numbers to a personal address?
options: Blocks or alerts on the message based on policy
questions.why: DLP inspects content leaving the organisation and enforces rules on sensitive data.

questions.q: What is data masking used for in testing environments?
options: Replacing real sensitive values with realistic fakes
questions.why: Developers can test with realistic data without seeing real personal information.

questions.q: What is anonymisation of data?
options: Removing identifying details so individuals can't be identified
questions.why: Properly anonymised data is no longer personal data, though re-identification can be a risk.

questions.q: What is pseudonymisation?
options: Replacing identifiers with tokens that can be re-linked using separate information
questions.why: Unlike anonymisation, the original identity can be restored by whoever holds the mapping.

questions.q: What is data retention policy?
options: Rules for how long different types of data must be kept and when to delete them
questions.why: Keeping data too long increases risk; deleting too soon can break legal requirements.

questions.q: What is geofencing in mobile security?
options: Using a device's location to allow or restrict actions
questions.why: For example, an app might only work while the device is on company premises.

questions.q: What is a security key (hardware token) used for?
options: As a physical second factor for authentication
questions.why: Security keys such as FIDO2 tokens prove possession and resist phishing.

questions.q: What is a time-based one-time password (TOTP)?
options: A code that changes every 30 seconds or so, generated by an app
questions.why: Authenticator apps compute TOTP codes from a shared secret and the current time.

questions.q: What is HOTP?
options: A one-time password based on a counter that increases with each use
questions.why: HOTP codes stay valid until used, unlike TOTP codes, which expire with time.

questions.q: What are the factors of authentication?
options: Something you know, have, are, and sometimes somewhere you are
questions.why: True MFA combines factors from different categories.

questions.q: What is a false rejection rate (FRR) in biometrics?
options: How often an impostor is accepted
How often a legitimate user is wrongly denied
questions.why: High FRR frustrates users; high false acceptance rate (FAR) weakens security.

questions.q: What is attribute-based access control (ABAC)?
options: Access set by the data owner
Access decisions based on attributes of the user, resource and environment
Access based only on job role
questions.why: ABAC can express rules like 'finance staff, on managed devices, during work hours'.

questions.q: What is mandatory access control (MAC)?
options: Access based on labels and clearances enforced by the system
Access based on time of day
Access decided by the data owner
questions.why: Users can't change MAC permissions; it's used in high-security environments.

questions.q: What is rule-based access control?
options: Access governed by system rules, such as firewall rules or time restrictions
questions.why: Rules apply to everyone equally, regardless of identity.

questions.q: What is time-of-day restriction?
options: Allowing logins only during set hours
questions.why: Logins outside approved hours are blocked, limiting misuse of stolen credentials.

questions.q: What is single sign-on (SSO)?
options: Using one password for every website
Logging in once to access many applications
Logging in with a fingerprint only
questions.why: SSO improves usability and centralises control, but the identity provider becomes a key target.

questions.q: What is SAML used for?
options: Exchanging authentication and authorisation assertions between an identity provider and a service
questions.why: SAML is an XML standard common for enterprise web single sign-on between an IdP and apps.

questions.q: What is LDAP used for?
options: Querying and managing directory information such as users and groups
questions.why: LDAP is how many applications look up accounts in directories like Active Directory.

questions.q: What is Kerberos's main purpose?
questions.why: Kerberos avoids sending passwords across the network by issuing time-limited tickets.

questions.q: Why does Kerberos need accurate time on all systems?
options: Tickets include timestamps and are rejected if clocks differ too much
questions.why: Time limits stop old tickets from being replayed, so clock skew causes failures.

questions.q: What is a service account?
options: An account used by an application or service rather than a person
questions.why: Service accounts often have high privileges and long-lived passwords, so they need careful control.

questions.q: Why are shared accounts discouraged?
options: Actions can't be traced to an individual
questions.why: Accountability requires knowing who did what.

questions.q: What is privilege escalation?
options: Gaining higher access rights than intended
questions.why: Attackers start with limited access and exploit flaws to become administrators.

questions.q: What is the purpose of reviewing user permissions regularly?
options: Removing access people no longer need
questions.why: Access reviews catch privilege creep and accounts left behind after role changes.

questions.q: What does the preparation phase of incident response include?
options: Building the plan, team, tools and training before incidents happen
questions.why: Preparation makes every later phase faster and more effective.

questions.q: What happens in the detection phase of incident response?
options: Identifying that an incident has occurred through alerts, logs or reports
questions.why: Detection triggers the response and starts analysis of scope and impact.

questions.q: What is the purpose of containment?
options: Stopping the incident from spreading or causing more damage
questions.why: Containment might isolate hosts, disable accounts or block IPs.

questions.q: What does recovery involve in incident response?
options: Restoring systems to normal operation and monitoring for problems
questions.why: Systems are brought back carefully, with extra monitoring for signs of reinfection.

questions.q: What is root cause analysis after an incident?
options: Finding the underlying reason the incident happened
questions.why: Fixing the root cause, not just symptoms, prevents repeats.

questions.q: What is the order of volatility used for?
options: Deciding which evidence to collect first because it disappears fastest
questions.why: Memory and network state vanish quickly, so they're captured before disk images.

questions.q: Why is chain of custody important in forensics?
options: It proves evidence was handled properly and not tampered with
questions.why: Gaps in custody can make evidence inadmissible in court.

questions.q: What is a forensic image?
options: A bit-for-bit copy of a storage device
questions.why: An exact copy, including deleted data, lets analysis happen without changing the original.

questions.q: Why is a hash taken of evidence when it is collected?
options: To prove later that it hasn't changed
questions.why: A matching hash at any later point shows the evidence is intact.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a lessons learned meeting?
options: To improve processes based on what happened during an incident
questions.why: Documenting what worked and what didn't strengthens the next response.

questions.q: What is threat hunting?
options: Proactively searching for hidden threats rather than waiting for alerts
questions.why: Hunters use hypotheses and data to find attackers who evaded automated detection.

questions.q: What is a security operations centre (SOC)?
options: A team and facility that monitors and responds to security events
questions.why: SOCs watch alerts around the clock and coordinate incident response.

questions.q: What is a playbook in security operations?
options: A documented set of steps for handling a specific type of event
questions.why: Playbooks make responses consistent, and SOAR tools can automate them.

questions.q: What does SOAR stand for?
questions.why: SOAR platforms connect tools and automate response playbooks.

questions.q: What does the NIST Cybersecurity Framework organise its functions into?
options: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
questions.why: CSF 2.0 added Govern to the original five functions.

questions.q: What is ISO/IEC 27001?
options: A standard for information security management systems that organisations can be certified against
questions.why: It sets requirements for an ISMS; ISO 27002 gives guidance on controls.

questions.q: What are the CIS Controls?
options: A prioritised set of practical security safeguards
questions.why: The Center for Internet Security publishes them to help organisations focus on the most effective defences.

questions.q: What is a benchmark such as a CIS Benchmark?
options: A detailed secure configuration guide for a specific product
questions.why: Benchmarks list recommended settings for systems like Windows, Linux and cloud services.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a business continuity plan (BCP)?
options: Keeping essential business functions running during and after a disruption
questions.why: A BCP covers people, processes and facilities; the DRP focuses on IT recovery.

questions.q: What is a disaster recovery plan (DRP)?
options: Procedures for restoring IT systems after a disaster
questions.why: The DRP is part of business continuity and focuses on technology.

questions.q: What does a business impact analysis identify?
options: Critical functions, their dependencies and the impact of their loss
questions.why: The BIA sets recovery priorities and objectives such as RTO and RPO.

questions.q: What is a single point of failure?
options: A component whose failure stops the whole system
questions.why: Redundancy, such as dual power supplies or clustered servers, removes single points of failure.

questions.q: What is failover testing?
options: Deliberately failing a component to confirm the backup takes over
questions.why: Untested failover often doesn't work when it's really needed.

questions.q: What is parallel processing as a recovery test?
options: Running the recovery site alongside production to confirm it works
questions.why: Parallel tests validate the alternate site without stopping primary operations.

questions.q: What is a simulation exercise in continuity planning?
options: A realistic walk-through that tests responses without causing real disruption
questions.why: Simulations sit between tabletop discussion and full failover tests.

questions.q: What is capacity planning in resilience?
options: Making sure there are enough people, technology and infrastructure to meet demand
questions.why: Planning for growth and peaks avoids outages caused by running out of resources.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of security awareness for remote workers?
options: Teaching safe practices for home networks, public Wi-Fi and device security
questions.why: Remote work moves the perimeter to homes and cafés, so user habits matter more.

questions.q: What is an insider threat?
options: A risk from people within the organisation, malicious or careless
questions.why: Insiders already have access, so monitoring, least privilege and offboarding are key.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a clean desk policy?
options: Preventing sensitive information being left visible or unattended
questions.why: Papers and notes left on desks can be read or taken.

questions.q: What is shoulder surfing?
options: Watching someone enter a password or PIN
questions.why: Privacy screens and awareness help prevent it.

questions.q: What is dumpster diving?
options: Searching discarded rubbish for useful information
questions.why: Shredding documents and destroying media stops attackers recovering them from the trash.

questions.q: What is pretexting?
options: Inventing a scenario to persuade someone to give information or access
questions.why: An attacker might pose as IT support or an auditor to sound legitimate.

questions.q: What is a business email compromise attack usually after?
options: Fraudulent payments or sensitive data through a trusted-looking email
questions.why: Attackers impersonate executives or suppliers and ask for urgent transfers.

questions.q: What is the best defence against invoice fraud from a spoofed supplier email?
options: Verifying payment changes by calling a known number
Replying to the email to confirm
Paying quickly to avoid late fees
questions.why: Out-of-band verification defeats spoofed or compromised email accounts.

questions.q: What is a deepfake risk in social engineering?
options: Fake audio or video of a trusted person used to authorise actions
questions.why: Attackers have used cloned voices of executives to request payments.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a non-disclosure agreement (NDA)?
options: Legally requiring parties to keep shared information confidential
questions.why: NDAs protect sensitive information shared with employees, contractors or partners.

questions.q: What is due diligence in third-party risk management?
options: Investigating a vendor's security and reliability before engaging them
questions.why: Due diligence finds red flags before you depend on the supplier.

questions.q: What is a supply chain risk with open-source libraries?
options: A compromised or vulnerable dependency can affect every application that uses it
questions.why: Tracking dependencies with a software bill of materials helps manage this.

questions.q: What is a software bill of materials (SBOM)?
options: A list of all components and libraries in a piece of software
questions.why: An SBOM lets you quickly check whether you're affected when a library vulnerability is announced.

questions.q: What is penetration testing's main difference from vulnerability scanning?
options: Pen testing tries to exploit weaknesses to show real impact
questions.why: Scanning finds possible issues; testers prove what an attacker could actually do.

questions.q: What is a red team?
options: A group that emulates real attackers to test defences
The team that defends the network
questions.why: Red teams test detection and response; blue teams defend; purple teams combine both.

questions.q: What is a blue team?
options: The defenders who monitor and protect systems
questions.why: Blue teams detect and respond to red team activity in exercises.

questions.q: What is passive reconnaissance?
options: Gathering information without directly interacting with the target's systems
questions.why: Public records, search engines and social media are passive sources.

questions.q: What is active reconnaissance?
options: Interacting directly with target systems, such as scanning them
questions.why: Active techniques can be detected and logged by the target.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the rules of engagement in a penetration test?
options: Defining scope, timing, methods and limits of the test
questions.why: Clear rules protect both the client and the testers.

questions.q: What is responsible disclosure?
options: Privately reporting a vulnerability to the vendor and giving time to fix it before publishing
questions.why: It balances informing the public with giving the vendor time to protect users.

questions.q: What is the purpose of security metrics such as mean time to patch?
options: Measuring how well security processes perform over time
questions.why: Metrics show where processes are slow and whether improvements work.

questions.q: What is a security champion programme?
options: Training staff in each team to promote good security practices
questions.why: Champions spread security knowledge and spot issues early in their own teams.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a privacy notice?
options: Telling people how their personal data is collected and used
questions.why: Privacy laws require transparency about data collection and use.

questions.q: What is data minimisation?
options: Collecting and keeping only the personal data that is needed
questions.why: Less data held means less to protect and less exposed in a breach.

questions.q: What does a cyber insurance policy do in risk management?
options: Transfers some financial risk of incidents to an insurer
questions.why: Insurance is risk transference; insurers often require basic controls first.

questions.q: What is residual risk?
options: The risk that remains after controls are applied
questions.why: No control removes all risk; residual risk must be within the organisation's appetite.

questions.q: What is inherent risk?
options: The level of risk before any controls are applied
questions.why: Comparing inherent and residual risk shows how much controls help.

questions.q: What is a risk owner?
options: The person accountable for managing a particular risk
The person who found the risk
questions.why: Each risk in the register needs an owner who decides and tracks the response.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a heat map in risk assessment?
options: Visually showing risks by likelihood and impact
questions.why: Risk heat maps help prioritise the high-likelihood, high-impact risks.
